title: Binomial normal forms and the intersection of Laurent rings
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $a\in R$, and $H_a=R[x,y]/(xy-a)$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Every element of $H_a$ has a unique expression $c_0+\sum_{i>0}c_i x^i+\sum_{j>0}d_j y^j$, with coefficients in $R$ and finitely many nonzero terms. Thus these monomials are an $R$-module basis [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Suppose additionally that $R$ is a domain and $a\ne0$, and write $K=\operatorname{Frac}R$, with rational function field $K(T)$ [def-weil-rational-function-field]. The homomorphism $H_a\to K(T)$ given by $x\mapsto T$ and $y\mapsto aT^{-1}$ is injective, its image is $R[T,aT^{-1}]$, and its fraction field is $K(T)$. Inside $K(T)$ its localizations at $x$ and $y$ are respectively $R[T,T^{-1}]$ and $R[aT^{-1},a^{-1}T]$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] [def-weil-laurent-polynomial-ring], and their intersection is $R[T,aT^{-1}]$. Under these additional hypotheses ($R$ a domain and $a\ne0$), if $R$ is a normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], then $H_a$ is a normal domain and every prime localization of $H_a$ is a normal domain [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. No Noetherianity assumption is imposed.

source.place: Agent coefficient normal-form and Laurent-intersection argument extracted from the assigned item, steps 1 and 3; supporting Tag 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and Tag 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain). The assertion about arbitrary a, including zero, is an agent monomial-reduction calculation.

proof.text: Put $P=R[x,y]$ and $I=(xy-a)$. Define an $R$-linear map $N:P\to P$ on monomials by $N(x^iy^j)=a^m x^{i-m}y^{j-m}$, $m=\min(i,j)$. Its image is the module $V$ of polynomials supported on $1,x^i\ (i>0),y^j\ (j>0)$, and it fixes $V$. For $m>0$ the identity $(xy)^m-a^m=(xy-a)\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(xy)^{m-1-r}a^r$ gives $x^iy^j-N(x^iy^j)\in I$; for $m=0$ this difference is zero. Extend linearly: every class in $P/I$ is represented by $N(p)\in V$.

source.place: Agent monomial-reduction and coefficient calculation for the assigned statement; normality inputs are Tags 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain).

proof.text: For each $i,j\ge0$, the defining formula gives $N(x^{i+1}y^{j+1})=aN(x^iy^j)$, since $\min(i+1,j+1)=1+\min(i,j)$. Therefore $N((xy-a)q)=0$ for every $q\in P$ by linearity. If two polynomials in $V$ represent the same class, their difference belongs to $I$ and is killed by $N$, but $N$ fixes that difference. They are equal, and equality is coefficientwise in $P$. Together with step 1 this proves unique finite-support coefficients over every commutative $R$ and the asserted basis. No cancellation by $a$ was used.

source.place: Agent monomial-reduction and coefficient calculation for the assigned statement; normality inputs are Tags 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain).

proof.text: Now assume $R$ is a domain and $a\ne0$. Evaluation $x\mapsto T$, $y\mapsto aT^{-1}$ in $K(T)$ kills $xy-a$, so it defines a homomorphism on the quotient: changing a representative by $(xy-a)q$ changes its value by zero. The normal form maps to $c_0+\sum_{i>0}c_iT^i+\sum_{j>0}d_ja^jT^{-j}$. Uniqueness of Laurent coefficients forces $c_0=c_i=d_ja^j=0$ if this value is zero. Since $R\hookrightarrow K$ and $a^j\ne0$, all $d_j$ vanish too. The map is injective, and its image is exactly $A=R[T,aT^{-1}]$ because the quotient is generated by $R,x,y$. Thus $H_a$ is a domain.

source.place: Agent monomial-reduction and coefficient calculation for the assigned statement; normality inputs are Tags 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain).

proof.text: The fraction field of $A\subset K(T)$ is $K(T)$. Indeed, for any fraction $P/Q$ with $P,Q\in K[T]$ and $Q\ne0$, write their finitely many coefficients as fractions of elements of $R$ and take the product $d\in R\setminus\{0\}$ of all denominators. Then $dP,dQ\in R[T]\subset A$, $dQ\ne0$, and $P/Q=(dP)/(dQ)$. Conversely a quotient of elements of $A$ with nonzero denominator is in $K(T)$.

source.place: Agent monomial-reduction and coefficient calculation for the assigned statement; normality inputs are Tags 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain).

proof.text: Put $U=aT^{-1}$. Inverting $x$ in the embedding of step 3 gives $A[T^{-1}]=R[T,T^{-1}]$, since $U=aT^{-1}$ already belongs to this ring. Inverting $y$ gives $A[U^{-1}]=R[U,U^{-1}]=R[aT^{-1},a^{-1}T]$, since $T=aU^{-1}$. These are the actual localizations: a fraction $h/x^m$ maps to $h(T,U)T^{-m}$ and a fraction $h/y^m$ to $h(T,U)U^{-m}$, respectively. Each map is injective because its denominator is nonzero in the field, and these displayed generators show surjectivity onto the indicated ring.

source.place: Agent monomial-reduction and coefficient calculation for the assigned statement; normality inputs are Tags 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain).

proof.text: Both rings of step 5 lie in $K[T,T^{-1}]$. For a finite Laurent sum $f=\sum_n c_nT^n$, membership in $R[T,T^{-1}]$ means $c_n\in R$ for every $n$. Writing $U^m=a^mT^{-m}$, membership in $R[U,U^{-1}]$ means $c_n\in a^{-n}R$ for every $n$: the coefficient of $U^{-n}$ must be $a^nc_n\in R$. For $n\ge0$, $R\subseteq a^{-n}R$, so the simultaneous condition is just $c_n\in R$. For $n=-j<0$, $a^jR\subseteq R$, so it is $c_{-j}\in a^jR$. These are precisely the sums $c_0+\sum_{i>0}c_iT^i+\sum_{j>0}d_ja^jT^{-j}$ with coefficients in $R$, hence precisely $A$ by step 3. This proves the intersection assertion without assuming normality or that $a$ is a unit.

source.place: Agent monomial-reduction and coefficient calculation for the assigned statement; normality inputs are Tags 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain).

proof.text: Assume now that $R$ is normal as well. The substitution $T\mapsto aT^{-1}=U$ is an involutive $K$-automorphism of $K(T)$, so $U$ is an indeterminate over $R$ and $R[U]$ is a polynomial ring just as $R[T]$ is. By the polynomial normality lemma both are normal domains. Apply the localization normality lemma to their nonzero elements $T$ and $U$: $B=R[T,T^{-1}]$ and $C=R[U,U^{-1}]$ are normal domains. Their fraction fields are $K(T)$: $A\subset B,C\subset K(T)$ and step 4 already shows every element of that field is a quotient from $A$.

source.place: Tags 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain); agent application to the two Laurent coordinate rings.

proof.text: If $z\in\operatorname{Frac}A=K(T)$ satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in $A$, the same equation has coefficients in $B$ and in $C$. Normality of these two domains in their common fraction field gives $z\in B$ and $z\in C$. Step 6 gives $z\in B\cap C=A$. Therefore $H_a\simeq A$ is a normal domain, by the definition of normality.

source.place: Agent monomial-reduction and coefficient calculation for the assigned statement; normality inputs are Tags 030A (lemma-polynomial-domain-normal) and 00GY (lemma-localize-normal-domain).

proof.text: Finally, for any prime $\mathfrak p$ of $H_a$, the multiplicative set $H_a\setminus\mathfrak p$ excludes zero. Apply the localization normality lemma to the normal domain just obtained and this set. Its localization is $(H_a)_{\mathfrak p}$ by the definition of localization at a prime, and is a normal domain. Neither normality input has a Noetherian hypothesis, so no such hypothesis is needed anywhere above.
